strengths: The paper presents an intuitive and potentially useful idea: interpreting a frozen foundation model's linear-probe weights through text-aligned concepts to identify possible spurious correlations.
The approach is lightweight and applies a common pipeline across both vision and text, with experiments on Waterbirds, CelebA, NICO++, and CivilComments.
Initializing probes from class-text embeddings and extracting human-readable concepts provides an accessible interface for model inspection.
The paper includes a useful discussion of practical limitations and cautions that discovered biases require human validation.
weaknesses: The central claim about exploiting weight 'drift' is not adequately supported. The main score uses only the final class weights and differences among classes; it does not directly use the initialization, displacement, or training trajectory. Consequently, the method is closer to interpreting learned linear-probe weights than analyzing drift. There is also no random-initialization or trajectory-based control.

The premise that an unbiased dataset would leave each learned weight equal to its class-name embedding is generally false: weights can move because class names incompletely represent visual or linguistic class variation, because the foundation model is imperfectly aligned, or because discriminative classification differs from semantic similarity. Thus, movement alone is not evidence of bias.

The quantitative evaluation does not directly measure bias-discovery quality. It lacks controlled experiments with known injected biases, concept-level precision/recall, human annotations, causal interventions, or tests distinguishing genuine spurious features from legitimate class attributes. Many reported concepts are generic, class-related, or difficult to interpret as biases.

The zero-shot prompting evaluation is potentially confounded by trying multiple discovered concepts and taking a maximum over templates. The paper does not adequately control for the number of candidate prompts, prompt-selection procedure, or gains obtainable from random/frequent concepts. Reported gains also lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run statistics.

Claims of universal accuracy improvement and state-of-the-art bias prevention overstate the results. Average accuracy falls substantially on Waterbirds (90.7 to 84.7) and CivilComments (83.4 to 69.0), while baseline coverage is very incomplete: most competing methods are evaluated on only one or two datasets, and no competing discovery method is reported for NICO++ or CivilComments.

Equation 3 subtracts the minimum similarity to another class. For multiclass classification, discrimination against the closest competing class would naturally involve the maximum competing similarity; using the minimum only shows preference over at least one class and can assign high scores to concepts that do not support the actual decision. This issue directly affects the multiclass NICO++ experiment.

The theoretical result is essentially a loose geometric triangle bound and does not establish that a highly ranked concept is present in the data, causally influences predictions, or corresponds to an undesirable correlation.

Important reproducibility and robustness details are missing, including seeds and variability, complete split/group definitions and label construction for CivilComments, training duration and stopping details, prompt aggregation/selection mechanics, and sensitivity to captioner, keyword extractor, vocabulary size, and foundation model. Overall, the idea is promising, but the current evidence is insufficient for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, intuitive pipeline for extracting human-readable concepts from the weights of a linear probe over frozen foundation-model embeddings.
The study spans image and text modalities and includes four datasets, comparisons with several recent bias-discovery approaches, and limited ablations of the scoring rule and concept-count cutoff.
Worst-group zero-shot accuracy improves over the unaugmented prompt on all four reported datasets, sometimes substantially.
The paper is generally readable, provides a correct cosine-similarity bound, and acknowledges limitations arising from captioning, keyword extraction, and ontology-based filtering.
weaknesses: The central claim is not convincingly evaluated. Prompt accuracy is only an indirect proxy for whether the extracted concepts are genuine biases; the paper provides no precision/recall evaluation against known spurious attributes, systematic human assessment, counterfactual intervention, or causal test of whether the concepts drive model decisions.

The claimed use of a weight-update trajectory is overstated: the principal score in Eq. 3 uses only the final classifier weights and does not depend on the initialization or trajectory. Consequently, the paper does not establish that class-text initialization or tracking drift is necessary. A random-initialization/no-initialization ablation and comparisons using intermediate checkpoints are missing.

The mathematical bound is a generic geometric inequality. It neither establishes that a concept is present in a sample nor shows that the concept causally influences predictions; those key premises are assumed rather than validated.

The zero-shot evaluation can favor methods returning more or better-tuned prompt candidates because predictions take a maximum over templates. Candidate budgets and prompt-selection protocols are not shown to be comparable across baselines. The cutoff of 15 is apparently selected empirically, but the tuning data and procedure are unspecified, creating a risk of test-set or benchmark-level overfitting.

The empirical comparisons are incomplete: most baselines are evaluated on only one or two datasets, leaving ConceptDrift without competing results on Nico++ and CivilComments. Relevant concept-based model-interpretability methods are also not meaningfully compared, weakening both novelty and state-of-the-art claims.

The paper repeatedly claims improved accuracy or bias prevention, yet average accuracy decreases on Waterbirds, Nico++, and especially CivilComments, where it falls from 83.4 to 69.0. No uncertainty estimates, significance tests, seed variation, or analysis of this severe tradeoff is provided.

Several extracted terms do not substantiate bias discovery. CivilComments outputs largely include toxicity indicators or identity terms that may be label-semantic rather than spurious; Nico++ outputs only partially recover the constructed contexts; and CelebA results contain generic appearance words. Describing new terms as biases merely because they score highly is unsupported.

Important experimental definitions and reproducibility details are missing, including the construction of worst groups for CivilComments and Nico++, CivilComments label/group processing, training duration, number of runs, seed sensitivity, prompt aggregation details, and a complete model-selection protocol. No code or resource release is indicated.

The novelty appears limited relative to prior concept-based interpretation: the main operation ranks text concepts by similarity differences to learned linear-classifier weights. The related-work discussion reduces alternatives to a small comparison table and does not establish why this constitutes a substantial technical advance.

The method conflates dataset correlations, model reliance, socially harmful bias, and ordinary class-predictive attributes. The brief broader-impact discussion does not adequately address the risks of automatically labeling sensitive identity terms as biases or the potential downstream harm from incorrect discoveries.

strengths: The paper proposes an intuitive and potentially useful direction: inspecting a linear probe’s weights to identify class-associated concepts rather than relying only on misclassified examples.
The approach is lightweight and broadly applicable when the foundation model provides aligned text and input embeddings.

Experiments cover both vision and language across four datasets, and the reported worst-group accuracy improvements are substantial, including 35.2% to 55.3% on Waterbirds and 33.1% to 53.7% on CivilComments.
The extracted concepts are qualitatively plausible in several cases, such as background terms for Waterbirds and gender-related terms for CelebA.
The presentation is generally clear, and the paper acknowledges limitations arising from captioning, keyword extraction, and ontology-based filtering.
weaknesses: The central framing is not matched by the algorithm: the proposed score uses only the final class weights and does not measure the claimed drift trajectory or even reference the initial text embeddings. The final-minus-initial score is instead treated as an inferior ablation. No random-initialization or alternative-initialization experiment establishes that drift from class-name embeddings is essential.

The premise that an unbiased dataset should leave the learned weights equal to the class-name embeddings is unsupported and generally unlikely because of modality gaps, class-name ambiguity, legitimate intra-class attributes, and distribution-specific structure. Consequently, a shifted weight need not indicate a spurious correlation.

Evaluation of bias discovery is mostly indirect. Prompted worst-group accuracy does not establish that the returned concepts are genuine biases, and there is no systematic comparison against ground-truth spurious attributes, human annotations, precision/recall, or faithfulness interventions on the trained probe.

The prompting protocol takes a maximum over bias-conditioned templates. This can reward generating more or more diverse candidates, and the paper does not control candidate counts across methods or clarify how prompt selection avoids test-set leakage. Thus, comparisons may conflate bias quality with prompt-search coverage.

Baseline coverage is incomplete: most competing methods are reported on only one or two datasets, while Nico++ and CivilComments have no competing bias-discovery results. Several table entries appear reused from prior work without a sufficiently detailed common evaluation protocol.

Reported worst-group gains frequently accompany meaningful average-accuracy losses, most notably 83.4% to 69.0% on CivilComments. The paper nevertheless makes broad claims of improved accuracy and bias prevention without analyzing this tradeoff or fairness metrics beyond worst-group accuracy.

The theoretical inequality is a generic geometric bound and does not show that highly scored concepts caused predictions, are present in the data reliably, or are spurious. It offers little support for the main identification claim.

The study reports no variability across seeds, confidence intervals, robustness to hyperparameters or captioners, class-name sensitivity, comparison with a probe initialized conventionally, or direct probe-level causal tests. These omissions make the empirical conclusions insufficiently convincing for a top-tier venue.

Reproducibility is limited by missing code or artifact information and underspecified dataset splits, group definitions, early-stopping details, prompt aggregation, baseline implementation, and concept-selection procedures.

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting and practically appealing shift from analyzing examples or errors to inspecting linear-classifier weights in a shared vision-language embedding space. The method is simple, scalable, and applicable to both image and text modalities.

The evaluation is ambitious in scope, covering Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, and ImageNet-1k. It considers downstream mitigation, zero-shot prompting, synthetic interventions, and transfer of discovered correlations across many ImageNet architectures.

The method and dynamic-thresholding procedure are presented clearly, with an algorithm, qualitative concept lists, and several ablations. The fully correlated setting targets a meaningful limitation of approaches that require observed counterexamples.
weaknesses: The central claim of detecting learned spurious correlations is not technically established. A classifier weight's similarity to a text embedding shows association, not that the concept was learned from the data or causally affects predictions. No theorem, weight-decomposition argument, or systematic intervention connects the proposed score to the paper's causal definition of spuriousness.

The class-neutral filtering is unreliable and exposes a definitional problem. Many reported ImageNet concepts are directly related to or visually confusable with their classes—for example, avocado and nachos for guacamole, firefighters and hydrants for fire trucks, shrimp and seafood for lobster, and markers or styluses for ballpoint pens. LLM or WordNet filtering cannot determine causal irrelevance, so these examples may be ordinary semantic context rather than spurious correlations.

There is no direct, comprehensive evaluation of SC identification precision or recall on benchmarks with known attributes or human annotations. The primary ImageNet validation uses only three selected correlations out of many discoveries. This small, apparently curated subset cannot support claims of broadly outperforming prior SC-discovery methods.

The synthetic-image intervention is heavily confounded. Adding text to a FLUX prompt can change composition, scale, style, visibility, and other image features besides the target concept. The paper provides no matched irrelevant-concept controls, blinded human verification, generator replication, or uncertainty estimates. Poor classification of generated composites therefore does not isolate the discovered concept as the cause.

Comparisons are incomplete and sometimes favor the proposed method. Several baselines are absent on entire datasets, Table 4 is qualitative, and zero-shot max-pooling may benefit methods that produce more prompts unless concept budgets are controlled. Moreover, the claimed zero-shot improvement masks substantial average-accuracy losses on CivilComments (80.2 to 71.0) and smaller losses on CelebA.

The fully spurious experiment is insufficiently specified: the construction and splits, number of runs, model-selection data, exact group evaluation, and access each method has to concepts are unclear. CelebA worst-group accuracy remains extremely low, and the mitigation results validate the combined discovery-plus-regularization pipeline rather than independently establishing discovery quality.

The score subtracts the minimum similarity over all classes, which in a 1000-class problem can be dominated by one unrelated anti-aligned class rather than genuine specificity to the target class. The knee-style threshold is also heuristic, with limited sensitivity analysis and no calibration or false-discovery study.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the stated code link is blank, ImageNet outputs are deferred until acceptance, and important details such as filtering prompts, random seeds, concept counts, synthetic-image verification, and full dataset transformations are missing. Negative correlations are defined but not meaningfully evaluated. Overall, the idea is promising, but the evidence does not yet substantiate the paper's strong causal and state-of-the-art claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: identifying learned shortcuts when labeled counterexamples are unavailable.
WASP is conceptually simple and potentially scalable, combining foundation-model embeddings, linear classifier weights, automated concept extraction, and dynamic selection.
The experiments cover both vision and language, including Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, and an exploratory ImageNet study.
The fully correlated benchmark provides some encouraging evidence: regularization using WASP concepts improves worst-group accuracy over ERM, GroupDRO, random concepts, and the reported LG baseline.
weaknesses: The central learned-spuriousness claim is not established. Although the narrative emphasizes weight drift from initialization, the score uses only the final weights rather than the change from the initial weights. There is no comparison against scores from the pretrained initialization or a random initialization, so ImageNet findings may simply reflect CLIP's pre-existing semantic geometry rather than correlations learned during fine-tuning.

The method does not truly transcend data analysis: its candidate inventory is extracted from dataset captions or input text. It therefore cannot discover a correlation absent from this data-derived inventory, contrary to the paper's broad framing.

The multiclass score subtracts the minimum similarity over classes. This does not measure class specificity: a concept can score highly for many classes provided it has low similarity to any one class. A maximum competing-class or appropriately normalized contrast would better match the stated intuition. This is especially consequential for ImageNet-1k.

The class-neutral filtering is unreliable. Reported candidates include 'avocado' for guacamole, 'shrimp/seafood/mussels' for American lobster, and 'osprey' for bald eagle. These are defining ingredients, visually similar categories, or closely related concepts rather than compelling spurious attributes. This undermines the operational definition of spuriousness.

The ImageNet evaluation is heavily selected and potentially confounded. Only three manually verified correlations receive quantitative evaluation; there is no precision estimate over randomly sampled discoveries, annotator protocol, random-concept baseline, or comparison across generators. Generated composite images may contain generator artifacts or visual proxies for the induced class, particularly shrimp versus lobster. Transfer to other classifiers does not show that WASP diagnosed those models' learned correlations.

The benchmark comparisons do not substantiate the claim of surpassing all state-of-the-art methods. Several cells are missing, methods operate under different modality constraints, DrML is not quantitatively compared, and the zero-shot intervention changes prompts using max pooling rather than directly measuring detection quality. CivilComments worst-group accuracy improves while average accuracy drops sharply from 80.2 to 71.0, a tradeoff that is not discussed.

Important experimental details are missing, including the smoothing-window value, construction and evaluation protocol for the fully spurious datasets, run counts or uncertainty for most results, and sensitivity to major pipeline choices such as captioner, keyword extractor, LLM filter, and foundation model.

The algorithm is internally inconsistent: it defines the dynamic cutoff as an index but then compares concept scores directly against that index. Negative correlations are introduced in the method but omitted from the formal algorithm and empirical evaluation.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the claims: the stated code link is blank, the full ImageNet outputs are deferred until acceptance, and core hyperparameters and selection details are absent. Overall, the idea is promising, but the current evidence does not support the paper's central claims at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: WASP offers a novel and practically useful perspective: it searches for learned correlations through classifier weights in a shared concept space, rather than relying exclusively on training-data statistics or validation errors.
The method is simple, scalable, and applicable across image and text modalities. Evaluations span Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, and ImageNet-1k.

The fully correlated setting is particularly compelling: WASP enables mitigation even when no training or validation counterexamples exist, improving worst-group accuracy substantially over ERM, GroupDRO, random-concept regularization, and the reported Lg baseline.

The ImageNet experiments provide striking evidence that discovered concepts can systematically affect predictions. Testing the generated examples across many independently trained architectures strengthens the case that some correlations reflect broad dataset shortcuts rather than an idiosyncrasy of one model.

The paper is clearly motivated and generally well presented, with an understandable algorithm, useful qualitative examples, a dynamic-threshold ablation, and explicit comparisons to several recent approaches.
weaknesses: The paper does not convincingly establish that all reported concepts are genuinely spurious under its own causal definition. Filtering with an LLM and WordNet is only a semantic heuristic, and examples such as firefighter–fire truck, shrimp–lobster, avocado–guacamole, kettle–coffeemaker, and crayons–eraser are meaningfully related to the target classes. Human annotation or an explicit causal-relevance evaluation is needed.

The quantitative ImageNet validation covers only three selected correlations and uses synthetic images. Adding a concept can change composition, scale, realism, and other generated-image properties; matched random-concept controls, multiple generators, blinded human verification, and evaluation over a larger randomly selected set of discoveries would make the causal claim substantially stronger.

Although the method is framed around weight drift, its score uses only the final classifier weights rather than the displacement from initialization. There is no ablation against random or standard initialization, direct ranking by the initial text weights, weight-difference scoring, or simple concept–label frequency/logit baselines, leaving the importance of the proposed weight-space mechanism under-isolated.

The zero-shot comparison may be affected by unequal numbers and qualities of prompts across methods: max pooling over more concepts creates additional opportunities for a high similarity. Results should control prompt count and report variability. Moreover, CivilComments worst-group accuracy improves at a sizable cost to average accuracy (80.2 to 71.0), which is understated.

Important reproducibility details are missing or unclear, including the smoothing window r, precise construction and splits for the 100%-correlated experiments, seed counts for all tables, LLM prompting/filtering details, and sensitivity to the captioner, encoder, keyword extractor, and filtering model. The manuscript also says full data will be released only upon acceptance, while the displayed code link is incomplete.

The evaluation lacks a direct discovery metric—such as precision/recall against annotated correlations, human-rated validity, or ranking quality—so downstream robustness improvements serve as an indirect and partly method-dependent proxy for SC-identification quality.
